title: Microstructural evolution and mechanical performance of CS1018 steel processed by additive friction stir deposition and subsequent heat treatment
abstract: Abstract Additive manufacturing (AM) has enabled rapid production of complex and high-performance metal components. In this study, the solid-state Additive Friction Stir Deposition (AFSD) process was demonstrated to deposit low-carbon steel CS1018. Process parameters were optimized to improve deposit quality and layer bonding. The AFSD process produced dense, metallurgically bonded CS1018 deposits with a refined ferrite–pearlite microstructure. Compared to the original CS1018 feedstock, the as-deposited material exhibited an ~ 18% lower hardness and ~ 11% lower tensile strength than the feedstock, accompanied by a ~ 78% increase in ductility. These changes are attributed to the AFSD-induced microstructural modifications: specifically, grain refinement and homogeneous dispersion of fine pearlite (Fe₃C) in a ferrite matrix. Post-deposition tempering at 210 °C and 518 °C produced only modest changes in hardness and tensile behavior relative to the as-deposited state. Changes in XRD peak breadth are consistent with reduced microstrain after tempering. Fractographic analysis revealed that the AFSD deposit’s fracture surface contained finer and more numerous dimples than the feedstock, consistent with its improved toughness. Overall, this work demonstrates that AFSD can successfully deposit low-carbon steel with good mechanical integrity. In addition, this work demonstrates that a moderate heat treatment can primarily serve to stabilize the microstructure and relief stresses without significantly altering the strength or hardness.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Additive Friction Stir Deposition (AFSD) has emerged as a promising solid-state additive manufacturing (AM) method, capable of processing various metal systems [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 – 4 ]. Distinct from conventional fusion-based AM technologies, AFSD avoids melting the feedstock material. Instead, it relies on frictional heat generated by a rotating consumable feedstock rod and severe plastic deformation to create dense, defect-free deposits that closely resemble wrought products [ 3 ]. The layer-by-layer construction process of AFSD, commercially known as MELD™, bypasses melt/solidification, thus mitigating common fusion-based AM issues like porosity and hot cracking. Additionally, AFSD can achieve high deposition rates, facilitating the fabrication of large-scale near net shape components [ 4 ,  5 ]. Due to these compelling benefits, industry sectors are actively investigating AFSD for applications involving aluminum, titanium, and various steel alloys [ 4 ].
Fig. 1 Schematic illustration of the AFSD process and experimental CS1018 deposition performed using a MELD L3 system

In AFSD, a rotating feedstock rod is pressed onto the substrate, producing frictional heat that softens the feedstock material [ 6 ]. This frictional heating, combined with the large downward force, causes the feedstock tip to become plasticized [ 7 ]. The plastically deformed material is subsequently deposited onto the substrate along a predefined tool path (based on G-code), undergoing significant stirring and forging action. Metallurgical bonds form between neighboring layers without melting, leading to fully dense builds. The detailed mechanism of AFSD and the specific MELD L3 equipment utilized in this research are illustrated in Fig.  1 . Upon reaching steady-state deposition conditions, multiple layers can be stacked to create three-dimensional components. Dynamic recrystallization during this solid-state layering process refines the microstructure, often resulting in ultrafine equiaxed grains and mechanical properties comparable or superior to conventionally processed wrought materials [ 3 ,  4 ].

Recently, AFSD has been successfully applied to various steel grades, including low-carbon, medium-carbon, and stainless steels. For instance, Lei et al. [ 8 ] demonstrated that AFSD of medium-carbon 1045 steel produced a remarkably fine-grained microstructure (~ 1–3 μm grain size) with tensile strengths surpassing 1100 MPa, a significant improvement over traditional processing methods due to dynamic recrystallization and severe deformation. Similar achievements were reported for stainless steels: Gotawala et al. [ 9 ] successfully deposited multilayers of SS304 with continuous dynamic recrystallization, achieving average tensile strengths around 692 MPa and exceptional ductility (~ 87% elongation). Agrawal et al. [ 10 ] observed ultrafine equiaxed grains (~ 5 μm), high densities of deformation-induced twins, and martensitic phases in SS316 deposits, leading to an advantageous combination of strength and ductility. Moreover, Gor et al. [ 4 ] confirmed AFSD’s capability to deposit complex duplex stainless steel (grade 2507), achieving a dual-phase microstructure with wrought-equivalent properties. Collectively, these findings highlight AFSD’s potential to produce high-quality ferrous components featuring refined microstructures and excellent mechanical performance. Recent studies have also demonstrated the capability of friction stir additive manufacturing to fabricate functionally graded metallic systems. For example, aluminium-based functionally graded materials produced by friction stir additive manufacturing exhibited strong correlations between processing conditions, microstructural evolution, and resulting mechanical properties. These findings further highlight the versatility of solid-state additive manufacturing approaches for tailoring material performance through process control [ 11 ].

Low-carbon steels, such as CS1018 (~ 0.18% C), are extensively utilized in industry due to their favorable machinability, weldability, and balanced strength. However, applying AFSD for additive manufacturing or repair of low-carbon steels like CS1018 remains relatively unexplored. The solid-state nature of AFSD is beneficial for such steels, as they typically avoid forming martensitic phases during cooling but can still significantly benefit from grain refinement. It is anticipated that AFSD would enhance microstructural refinement and toughness in CS1018, similar to those improvements observed in higher-carbon steels [ 8 ], despite the reduced martensite-based strengthening mechanisms. To ease the deposition starting process, this study employed a heated substrate, capable of achieving 650 °C initial temperature, as suggested by Asiatico [ 12 ]. Such preheating aids in promoting robust initial layer bonding and minimizing thermal gradients. Although AFSD is a solid-state process, localized regions may momentarily approach the austenitizing temperature range (870–940 °C) due to severe plastic deformation and frictional heating. While localized temperatures beneath the tool may approach the A1/A3 range depending on process conditions, CS1018’s low carbon content (~ 0.18 wt%) makes the formation of significant martensite fractions unlikely under typical AFSD thermal cycles. Thus, the primary microstructural evolution is expected to involve ferrite–pearlite refinement, recovery/recrystallization, and possible transient austenite formation followed by transformation back to ferrite–pearlite, rather than martensite-based strengthening.

Post-deposition heat treatments of steel parts were also explored to relieve residual stresses and optimize mechanical properties, commonly practiced in fusion-based AM. Dolzhenko et al. [ 13 ] showed that friction-stirred higher-carbon steels initially containing martensitic structures benefited significantly from optimized tempering treatments, enhancing toughness by achieving tempered martensitic or ferritic microstructures. Since AFSD-deposited low-carbon steel CS1018 generally presents a ferrite–pearlite microstructure rather than martensite, moderate tempering (400–600 °C) can alleviate residual stresses without significantly altering phases and stabilize the refined microstructure, ensuring dimensional stability and balanced mechanical performance [ 13 ].

Despite the promising capabilities of AFSD, processing hard metals, such as low-carbon steel CS1018, presents considerable challenges. First, steels typically exhibit higher flow stress at elevated temperatures compared to lighter aluminum alloys, demanding greater frictional heating and force to achieve adequate plasticity deformation during AFSD [ 6 ,  14 ]. Careful thermal management is essential since inadequate heating prevents sufficient plasticization, whereas excessive heat risks damaging tools or substrates [ 6 ]. Studies have highlighted strategies such as substrate preheating or supplemental heat sources to manage these issues effectively [ 6 ]. High forging forces required in AFSD pose limitations for depositing thin-walled features and necessitate robust machine design [ 6 ]. In addition, achieving strong metallurgical bonding in AFSD-deposited steel layers is complicated by the formation of persistent oxide layers at elevated temperatures [ 4 ,  15 ]. If these oxides remain intact, they hinder effective inter-layer bonding, resulting in potential defects like weak “kissing bonds” or inter-layer voids [ 4 ]. Research on stainless steel deposition has demonstrated that proper surface preparations, such as machining between layers or maintaining inert conditions, are essential to prevent oxide-induced weak interfaces [ 15 ]. Finally, microstructural control during AFSD of steel remains challenging. The severe deformation and dynamic recrystallization inherent in AFSD frequently yield ultrafine or nanocrystalline grain structures [ 14 ]. Ensuring uniformity and avoiding undesirable phase transformations demand precise optimization of processing parameters. Rapid thermal cycling or high strains during deposition can inadvertently introduce localized tempered martensitic phases, complicating microstructural consistency [ 6 ,  14 ]. Ongoing research continues to refine parameter optimization strategies, aiming to reliably produce defect-free steel deposits with desirable microstructures and properties [ 4 ].

Although AFSD of steels has been reported, most published studies emphasize medium-/higher-carbon steels and stainless steels where strengthening/transformation mechanisms differ substantially from low-carbon grades. For CS1018, the response is expected to be dominated by removal of feedstock cold-work strengthening, ferrite–pearlite refinement, and interfacial oxidation effects on bonding. In addition, graphite-assisted feeding may introduce carbon pickup that can alter pearlite fraction and yield-point behavior, but this is rarely quantified for CS1018 AFSD builds. Therefore, this work establishes a reproducible process route for CS1018 AFSD and evaluates the process–structure–property evolution in the as-deposited and tempered states. This study examines the AFSD process for depositing CS1018 steel, including the influence of subsequent heat tempering treatments on microstructure and mechanical characteristics. Experimental methods, mechanical and microstructural analysis results, and their implications within the existing literature are presented and discussed in subsequent sections, culminating in key conclusions outlined in Sect.   4 . Detailed quantification is recognized as important for fully resolving carbon pickup and oxidation effects, but is left as future work in the present study. To the authors’ knowledge, a systematic investigation of AFSD-processed CS1018 steel combined with post-deposition tempering and comprehensive microstructure-property characterization has not been previously reported.

In this study, we aim to: (1) establish a reproducible AFSD processing route for CS1018 low-carbon steel, (2) quantify the resulting changes in microstructure and mechanical properties in the as-deposited and tempered states, and (3) assess the effectiveness of moderate tempering (210 °C and 518 °C) in stabilizing the AFSD microstructure without degrading mechanical performance.

sections.heading: Feedstock materials
paragraphs: Commercial CS1018 low-carbon steel was used as both feedstock and substrate. The feedstock was supplied in a cold-drawn condition to represent an industrially relevant starting state and to enable direct comparison between a work-hardened baseline and the AFSD-processed material. Feedstock rods were square bars with a cross-section of 9.5 mm × 9.5 mm and length of 457 mm. The substrate was a CS1018 plate with dimensions approximately 305 mm × 102 mm × 12.7 mm.
The nominal chemical composition of CS1018 is provided in Table  1  (ASTM A108).

sections.heading: AFSD processing and fabrication parameters
paragraphs: Prior to deposition, the substrate surface was mechanically abraded using abrasive paper to remove loose contaminants. No additional oxide removal or chemical cleaning treatment was applied. A thin graphite lubricant was applied only to the feedstock surface to reduce adhesion to the tool during feeding.

A four-layer block was fabricated using a bidirectional toolpath along the same deposition line. Each layer was deposited along the same coordinate path, and the traverse direction was reversed between successive layers. The total build height was approximately 2 mm, and the deposition length was about 178 mm. Substrate temperature was monitored using K-type thermocouples embedded beneath the substrate near the deposition start location. The measured temperature represents the substrate response rather than the instantaneous peak temperature directly beneath the rotating tool. A MELD L3 additive friction stir deposition machine was used, equipped with a water-cooled spindle and a standard MELD tungsten tool. The deposition tool had an outer diameter of 38.1 mm and featured a flat circular frontal surface without protrusions, serving to contain and forge the plasticized CS1018 material during deposition. During operation, the feedstock rod was advanced toward the substrate through the rotating tool. Upon contact, frictional heating softened the feedstock rod tip, and material began to flow out and deposit onto the substrate. After initial material fill and “spot” formation, the tool traversed according to a programmed toolpath to build the part layer by layer. The successful deposition of CS1018 steel via AFSD required careful process optimization due to the difficulty of controlling plasticity of hard metals like steels. Spindle speed, feed rate, traverse speed, and layer thickness were systematically varied to balance heat generation, material flow, and bonding quality. Table  2  summarizes the adopted parameters, with spindle speeds of 500 RPM, feed rates of 0.4 mm/s, an average tool power of 4900 W, and traverse speeds of 2.7 mm/s for a nominal layer height of 0.5 mm. The selection was guided by an empirical formula balancing the volumetric input and deposition rates. This approach enabled the fabrication of fully dense, high-quality CS1018 deposits.

Following process optimization, the as-deposited CS1018 was compared to the original feedstock. Microstructural analysis revealed finer ferrite–pearlite structures and improved homogeneity in the AFSD deposit. Mechanical testing showed that AFSD processing increased tensile elongation relative to the CS1018 feedstock, while slightly reducing strength and hardness. This behavior reflects a transition from the initial feedstock condition to a fine-grained, annealed-like ferrite–pearlite microstructure produced by solid-state processing, rather than an intrinsic strengthening effect. As such, AFSD primarily redistributes mechanical properties, favoring ductility and toughness at the expense of strength, which may be beneficial for applications where damage tolerance is prioritized.

where  a  is the side of the feedstock cross-section,  ẏ  is the feedstock feed rate,  w  is the deposited layer width,  t  is the deposited layer thickness, and  ẋ  is the traverse velocity [ 7 ]. After resetting the tool position and preheating the substrate, deposition was performed to create a multi-layered CS1018 block approximately 2 mm in height (4 layers). To prevent jamming, a thin layer of graphite lubricant was applied to the surface of the feedstock rods to reduce adhesion to the tool.
Fig. 2 Heated substrate setup used to preheat the CS1018 substrate to 650 °C prior to deposition

After setting the positions of the tool, the substrate was preheated to 650 °C using an integrated heater (Fig.  2 ) to promote bonding of the first layer and reduce thermal gradients. During deposition, the local temperature beneath and behind the rotating tool is expected to be higher due to additional frictional heating, as indicated by the increased radiance observed in the tool wake in Fig.  1 . Substrate temperature was monitored using embedded thermocouples, while transient peak temperatures directly under the tool were not measured.

sections.heading: Post-Processing and Mechanical Testing
paragraphs: Two post-deposition tempering treatments were applied to the AFSD CS1018 samples to evaluate their effects relative to the thermal exposure experienced during deposition. The first treatment consisted of a low-temperature stress-relief temper at 210 °C for 1 h, while the second involved a higher-temperature temper at 518 °C for 1 h with a heating rate of 10 °C/min, followed by furnace cooling. These treatments represent significantly longer dwell times at lower temperatures compared to the brief, but higher-temperature thermal exposure associated with the 650 °C substrate preheat and the localized frictional heating during AFSD. As a result, the tempering cycles primarily promote stress relief and microstructural stabilization rather than the rapid thermal effects occurring during deposition. These two conditions were chosen to evaluate the effect of minimal vs. moderate tempering on the AFSD prepared CS1018 microstructure and illusrated in Fig.  3 .

Fig. 3 Schematic representation of the post-deposition tempering cycles applied to AFSD CS1018 samples, including 210 °C and 518 °C treatments with a heating rate of 10 °C/min, 1 h hold time, and furnace cooling

The 210 °C treatment is expected to relieve some residual stress with negligible microstructural change, while the 518 °C treatment (near the lower end of typical tempering for higher-carbon steels) could further relieve stress and slightly temper microstructural features (e.g., temper any potential martensite or modify carbide dispersion [ 13 ]).
Fig. 4 Geometry and dimensions of the subsize tensile specimen used for mechanical testing (in mm)

The as-deposited block was sectioned to produce specimens for mechanical testing and metallography. A wire EDM (electrical discharge machining) was used (Sodick AQ300L, Fig.  4 ) to avoid inducing mechanical stress or heating during cutting [ 18 ]. Subsize tensile specimens of “dogbone” geometry (gauge length ~ 25 mm, width ~ 6 mm, thickness ~ 2 mm) were extracted from the center of the deposit (along the layer deposition direction) as well as from the original CS1018 feedstock bar for baseline comparison. Figure  4  shows the dimensions of the dogbone shaped tensile coupons. Three tensile coupons were prepared from the deposit (as-deposited condition) and three from the feedstock. Additionally, for each heat treatment condition, at least three tensile specimens were tempered after machining. All tensile specimens were tested in the as-machined surface condition (no further polishing was done on the gauge area). (Figure  5 ).
Fig. 5 ( a ) Schematic illustration of tensile specimen extraction locations from the deposited material. ( b ) Tensile specimens extracted from AFSD-processed CS1018 deposits and feedstock material

Vickers microhardness measurements were performed from the top surface of the deposit toward the substrate along the build direction. For consistency, multiple indents (at least 3) were made in each region and averaged. Tensile tests were performed at room temperature using a load frame equipped with a 5 kN load cell. Tests were conducted under displacement control at a crosshead rate of 0.5 mm/min. Because no extensometer was used, engineering strain was estimated from crosshead displacement (thus it is approximate). For each condition, at least three specimens were tested, and results were reported as mean values. Fractured tensile specimens were examined via SEM to characterize the fracture surface morphology.

sections.heading: Materials characterization
paragraphs: For microstructural analysis, samples were cut from the deposit both in the as-deposited state and after each tempering treatment. These samples were sectioned vertically (parallel to the build direction) to examine the through-thickness (layered) microstructure. Standard metallographic preparation procedure was performed, through which the samples were mounted in bakelite, ground with SiC papers, and polished with alumina suspension to a mirror finish. Nital (5% nitric acid in ethanol) etching was used to reveal the ferrite–pearlite microstructure. The etched samples were observed under an optical microscope and a scanning electron microscope (SEM). Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping was conducted on selected areas to check for elemental uniformity (particularly to detect any tungsten tool debris or other contaminants, and to examine carbon distribution qualitatively between ferrite and pearlite). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was performed at 20 kV to examine the microstructure and elemental distribution using energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). EBSD analyses were conducted on a Thermo Fisher Helios G5 Xe PFIB/SEM at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV and a probe current of 1.6 nA. Grain size was determined from EBSD orientation maps using the equivalent circular diameter (ECD) method with a 10° misorientation threshold.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed for phase identification using a PANalytical Empyrean diffractometer with a Cu anode (Kα1 = 1.5406 Å, Kα2 = 1.5444 Å) operated at 45 kV and 40 mA. Data were collected in continuous scan mode with a step size of 0.013° (2θ) and analyzed over a 2θ range of 20–100°.

sections.heading: Deposition optimization
paragraphs: The additive deposition trials on CS 1018 steel encompassed a range of process parameters aimed at eliminating defects and improving layer adhesion. Figure  6  illustrates the progression of deposit quality under these varied conditions. Early trials using thicker layers (1 mm), higher feed rates (50 mm/min), and faster travel speeds (up to 4.4 mm/s) led to excessive flash formation and poor surface finishes. By systematically refining the parameters – specifically, reducing the layer thickness to 0.5 mm, lowering the feed rate to 25 mm/min, and decreasing the travel speed to 160 mm/min – the deposited tracks became far more consistent with a smoother surface. Table  3  summarizes the key parameter sets evaluated during the optimization stage and their corresponding deposition outcomes.

Fig. 6 CS1018 deposited parts produced under different AFSD processing conditions during process optimization: ( a ) Trial 1 (1.0 mm L.T, 50.82 mm/min F.R, 400 RPM S.S, and 264.18 mm/min T.S.), ( b ) Trial 2 (1.0 mm layer thickness, 30.48 mm/min F.R, 500 RPM S.S, and 228.6 mm/min T.S), ( c ) Trial 3 (0.75 mm L.T, 30.48 mm/min F.R, 500 RPM S.S, and 198.12 mm/min T.S), and ( d ) Trial 4 (0.5 mm L.T, 22.8 mm/min feed rate, 500 RPM S.S, and 198.12 mm/min T.S).( e ) Trial 5 (0.5 mm L.T, 25.38 mm/min feed rate, 500 RPM S.S, and 198.12 mm/min T.S.), ( f ) Optimized condition (0.5 mm L.T, 24 mm/min F.R, 500 RPM S.S, and 162 mm/min T.S.)

The reduction in layer thickness and feed rate improved material flow stability and reduced flash formation. The optimized deposition condition produced a flat top surface with smooth, continuous layers and no visible large-scale defects. This parameter set was therefore selected for making samples for the subsequent microstructural characterization and mechanical testing presented in this study. The optimized parameter set was selected based on visual inspection of deposit quality, reduction of flash formation, absence of visible bonding defects, and achievement of continuous deposition.

sections.heading: Deposition process data analysis
paragraphs: Figure  6  presents the processing data recorded by the machine during the deposition of four layers. The torque and force curves display sharp initial peaks at the moment of tool engagement, which is expected due to the sudden resistance of the cold feedstock to plastic deformation [ 7 ,  13 ]. The power curve mirrors these trends, with a high initial input required to overcome the static resistance and then a stable energy demand that reflects efficient, balanced energy conversion during continuous deposition [ 2 ,  9 ].

The temperature profile shown in Fig.  7  rises sharply immediately after tool–substrate contact due to rapid frictional heating and intense plastic deformation at the interface. The measured temperature reflects the response of the embedded thermocouple and should be interpreted as a substrate-proximal value rather than the peak temperature directly beneath the tool. After this initial rise, the temperature stabilizes at approximately 580 °C, demonstrating sufficient thermal input to sustain plastic flow and promote metallurgical bonding during deposition [ 2 ,  7 ]. Only two dominant temperature peaks are observed because the thermocouple was embedded beneath the substrate near the starting location, while deposition followed a continuous back-and-forth tool path; consequently, elevated temperatures were recorded only when the tool passed close to the thermocouple. In contrast, torque, force, and power exhibit four peaks corresponding to each deposited layer. Substrate heating was turned off prior to deposition, so the measured temperature does not reach the nominal 650 °C preheat value, and the machine operated continuously without stopping between direction changes. The four-layer build took approximately 4 min 10 s.
Fig. 7 Process data recorded during four-layer AFSD deposition of CS1018: ( a ) actuator torque, ( b ) axial force, ( c ) deposition power, and ( d ) substrate temperature

sections.heading: Hardness and tensile properties
paragraphs: Figure  8  summarizes the hardness and tensile properties for the CS1018 feedstock, the as-deposited AFSD material, and the samples tempered at 210 °C and 518 °C. All mechanical test specimens were taken from the central, well-bonded region of the deposits to ensure that the measured properties reflect the fully consolidated material. The as-deposited AFSD CS1018 shows a noticeable reduction in hardness and strength accompanied by a large increase in ductility compared to the original feedstock. Specifically, the as-deposited material’s Vickers microhardness is about 18% lower than the feedstock (dropping from ~ 206 HV in the feedstock to ~ 170 HV in the deposit), and the tensile strength decreased on the order of 10% (e.g., a drop in ultimate strength from approximately 622 MPa to 554 MPa). In contrast, ductility improved markedly: the as-deposited sample attained ~ 32% total elongation, roughly a 78% increase over the feedstock’s elongation. The reported hardness values represent the average of measurements taken along the build direction from the top surface toward the substrate. All reported values correspond to the mean ± standard deviation, calculated from at least three tests per condition.

Tempering the AFSD deposits at 210 °C and 518 °C resulted in only minor changes to mechanical properties relative to the as-deposited state. The 210 °C tempered sample had virtually the same hardness as the as-deposited material (within experimental scatter), indicating that this low-temperature heat treatment relieved some residual stresses with negligible softening effect.

The 518 °C tempered sample showed a slight further reduction in hardness and strength compared to the as-deposited condition, consistent with a modest annealing effect at the higher tempering temperature. However, even at 518 °C, the changes were not dramatic – strength and hardness remained on the same order as the untampered deposit, confirming that no significant phase transformations or over-tempering occurred. Ductility in both tempered conditions remained high. The 210 °C temper maintained the elongation near ~ 30%, and the 518 °C temper perhaps allowed a modest additional increase in ductility due to stress relief (though any increase was small given the already high ductility of the as-deposited material). All tested conditions exhibited ductile behavior, and the yield point phenomenon characteristic of low-carbon steel was observed in each case. Notably, the as-deposited and tempered samples showed discontinuous (serrated) yielding during tensile tests. This is associated with Lüders band formation in low-carbon steels: the fine-grained AFSD microstructure introduces a high density of grain boundaries that impede dislocation motion and the propagation of Lüders bands, producing a serrated stress–strain response [ 19 ]. Low-carbon steels are more likely to develop Lüders bands than alloys like titanium and aluminum. The reason is that work hardening makes the plastic flow smoother and more consistent after the material yields by preventing localized strain accumulation or strain aging [ 20 ].

Fig. 8 Mechanical properties of CS1018 feedstock and AFSD-processed material: ( a ) Vickers microhardness results, ( b ) engineering stress–strain curves comparing feedstock and as-deposited conditions, ( c ) engineering stress–strain curves for the 210 °C tempered condition, and ( d ) engineering stress–strain curves for the 518 °C tempered condition

sections.heading: Microstructure evaluation
paragraphs: Cross-sectional microscopy and EDS analysis were performed to compare the internal microstructure and layer bonding in the feedstock, as deposited, and tempered samples. Layer bonding quality was evaluated for the as-deposited and tempered builds. No large-scale defects were observed at the examined magnification, and the layers appeared well bonded at the investigated scale. As shown in Fig.  9 a–b, excellent metallurgical bonding is observed in the central region of each layer, extending beyond the original feedstock rod width, which indicates effective material spreading and forging under the tool. Small lack-of-bond regions are present at the extreme side edges of some layers; these regions remain within the tool footprint, while the flash extends laterally beyond the tool contact surface. EDS oxygen mapping suggests that localized oxidation contributed to the reduced bonding at the layer edges. EDS results revealed a higher concentration of oxygen along these side interface regions, suggesting that oxidation during deposition contributed to locally weaker bonding (the trapped oxides can prevent intimate metal-to-metal contact).
Fig. 9 ( a - b ) Cross-sectional evaluation of interlayer bonding in AFSD CS1018 deposits showing side-edge and center regions together with corresponding EDS elemental maps

In the tempered conditions, these as-deposited interface characteristics remained largely unchanged. The 210 °C tempering is too low to affect any oxide films or to enable diffusion bonding across a gap, so the minor edge gaps and oxides persist in the 210 °C tempered sample. The 518 °C tempering, while hotter, also did not alter the interfacial oxide – no evidence of new metallurgical bonding was found at those pre-existing gap locations after heat treatment. (Any healing of voids or cracks would require higher temperatures or deformation to recur at the interface, which were not part of the tempering process.) Nevertheless, the bulk of the AFSD material was well-bonded: the central area interfaces remained intact after tempering, and no new defects were introduced by the heat treatments.

The feedstock (baseline CS1018 steel) exhibits a typical ferrite–pearlite microstructure consistent with its low carbon content of approximately 0.15–0.20 wt%. The ferrite grains are relatively coarse, and the pearlite area fraction is around 17%, which aligns well with the expected equilibrium composition for CS1018 steel. The pearlite fraction was estimated from image analysis of etched micrographs and is therefore reported as area fraction. (Figure  10 ).

Fig. 10 SEM images of CS1018  (a)  Feedstock,  (b)  AFSD as-fabricated,  (c)  210 °C Heat treated sample,  (d)  518 °C Heat treated sample,  (e)  EDS mapping of 210 °C Heat treated sample,  (f)  EDS mapping of 518 °C Heat treated sample

The as-deposited AFSD CS1018 steel has a much finer and more uniform microstructure than the original feedstock. The feedstock shows the typical ferrite–pearlite structure of low-carbon steel, with larger ferrite grains and pearlite colonies. In comparison, the AFSD-deposited material has small, evenly shaped ferrite grains and evenly spread pearlite colonies, showing that significant grain refinement occurs during deposition. Both the feedstock and deposited layers lack continuous cementite networks, which matches the low carbon content of CS1018 steel.

Image analysis shows that the deposited material contains about 31% pearlite, while the feedstock has around 17%. The higher pearlite fraction may result from carbon redistribution and improved pearlite visibility in the refined microstructure. The strong plastic deformation during AFSD breaks up and spreads out cementite particles, leading to a finer and more even ferrite–pearlite structure. This refined structure is similar to what has been seen in steels processed by other friction stir-based solid-state methods.

Heat treatments at 210 °C and 518 °C do not greatly change the overall ferrite–pearlite structure of the AFSD material. The sample tempered at 210 °C keeps a microstructure almost the same as the as-deposited state, with no visible phase changes and only slight differences in ferrite grain shape or pearlite distribution.

The sample heat-treated at 518 °C keeps the ferrite–pearlite structure of the deposited material, though the pearlite lamellae become slightly coarser and some spheroidization occurs after one hour of tempering. Even with these small changes, the overall structure stays stable, with no signs of martensite or other new phases. X-ray diffraction shows that all samples are mainly made up of ferrite (α-Fe) and cementite (Fe₃C). EDS elemental maps also show no major changes in composition across the deposited layers, so the chemical makeup is very similar to the original CS1018 feedstock.
Fig. 11 EBSD inverse pole figure (IPF) maps of CS1018 in the feedstock, as-deposited AFSD, 210 °C tempered, and 518 °C tempered conditions

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) inverse pole figure (IPF) orientation maps provided more details about the grain structure. The feedstock has fairly large ferrite grains with big orientation areas, while the as-deposited AFSD material shows much finer, more evenly shaped grains with many grain boundaries. After heat treatment at 210 °C, the grain structure is still much like the as-deposited state, with negligible grain growth. In comparison, the sample treated at 518 °C shows a small increase in grain size, but the grains are still much finer than those in the feedstock. Grain size measurements from EBSD analysis indicate average grain sizes of approximately ~ 5 μm for the feedstock, ~ 3 μm for the as-deposited condition, ~ 3.3 μm after 210 °C heat treatment, and ~ 3.7 μm after 518 °C heat treatment. These findings confirm that AFSD processing achieves significant grain refinement in CS1018 steel, while subsequent heat treatments cause only moderate grain coarsening without altering the overall ferrite–pearlite phase structure.

sections.heading: XRD results
paragraphs: X-ray diffraction was utilized to compare phase composition and lattice characteristics of the feedstock, as-deposited, and tempered CS1018 samples. The XRD pattern of the CS1018 feedstock (Fig.  12 ) shows sharp peaks corresponding to the body-centered cubic ferrite (α-Fe) phase, consistent with its wrought condition. The narrow peak widths indicate a relatively coarse grain size and low internal strain in the feedstock. No additional phases were detected, which is expected given the low carbon content and ferrite–pearlite microstructure of CS1018 steel. The XRD patterns confirmed that all conditions are dominated by the ferrite (α-Fe, BCC) phase. Although CS1018 steel contains a ferrite–pearlite microstructure with cementite (Fe₃C), distinct cementite peaks are not clearly detectable in Fig.  11  due to their low volume fraction. In the feedstock, distinct peaks corresponding to α-Fe (such as the (110), (200), and (211) reflections of BCC iron) are observed with intensities typical of a ferrite–pearlite steel. The as-deposited AFSD sample shows the same set of ferrite peaks and no new diffraction peaks, indicating that the solid-state deposition did not introduce any martensite or other allotropic phases despite the severe deformation. This peak broadening indicates increased lattice strain and reduced coherent domain size in the as-deposited material. Similarly, the tempered samples (210 °C and 518 °C) exhibit the same ferritic XRD peaks with only slight variations in peak profile, and no additional phases. Notably, there were no peaks corresponding to iron oxides detectable in the bulk XRD patterns, even though some oxide was found at layer interfaces via EDS – this suggests the oxides are present only in trace amounts or as very thin films at interfaces (below XRD detection threshold), and the overall phase makeup of the material remains unchanged after tempering.

Fig. 12 XRD patterns of CS1018 steel in the feedstock, as-deposited (AFSD), and tempered (210 °C and 518 °C) conditions. Measurements were performed on a Empyrean diffractometer (θ/θ geometry, reflection–transmission spinner) using Cu Kα radiation (45 kV, 40 mA). Patterns are shown over 2θ = 20–100° with step size 0.01313°. Peak markers correspond to α-ferrite (BCC Fe) reflections: (110), (200), (211), and (220)

While the phase composition remained constant, comparative analysis of the XRD peak profiles provides insight into microstructural differences and residual stress relief among the conditions. The feedstock’s diffraction peaks are relatively sharp, consistent with its coarse grain size and low internal strain (the feedstock bar was likely in a cold-worked or minimally stressed state). In the as-deposited material, the ferrite peaks appear slightly broadened. Additionally, any residual stresses from the deposition process could cause minor shifts in peak positions. After 210 °C tempering, the diffraction peaks of the AFSD steel narrowed subtly compared to the untampered condition. The overall peak positions for ferrite in the 210 °C sample remained essentially the same, indicating that any residual stress present in the as-deposited state was partially reduced but not eliminated by this mild temper. The 518 °C tempered sample’s XRD peaks were noticeably sharper and more defined than those of the as-deposited sample. In summary, the XRD results demonstrate that post-deposition tempering primarily affects the peak width (and thus macrostrain/grain size) rather than the peak positions or the fundamental phases present. sections.heading: Fracture surface
paragraphs: Fractographic analysis of tensile specimens demonstrated ductile failure modes in both feedstock and deposited materials. The feedstock showed large, widely spaced dimples. In contrast, the as-deposited AFSD sample’s fracture surface is covered by much finer and more uniformly distributed dimples. This microvoid distribution is consistent with the higher ductility observed in the as-deposited material [ 9 ,  13 ]. The tempered AFSD samples also exhibited ductile fracture features and retained the fine dimple morphology. The fracture surfaces of the 210 °C and 518 °C tempered specimens closely resembled that of the as-deposited material, with an abundance of small, equiaxed dimples. The uniformly and closely spaced dimples in the tempered conditions indicate that the heat treatments did not significantly alter the ductile fracture behavior of the AFSD steel. In the 210 °C tempered sample, dimples remained tiny and densely packed, showing that the fine microstructure (and thus high void nucleation site density) was preserved. The 518 °C tempered sample’s dimples were also predominantly small and round, though a few dimples appeared marginally larger than those in the untampered deposit. Overall, all AFSD-processed samples (as-fabricated and tempered) failed in a ductile manner with extensive micro void coalescence. The fracture surfaces of the AFSD specimens exhibited predominantly ductile features, characterized by micro void coalescence and a dimpled morphology. No large-scale lack-of-bond defects were observed at the magnification examined. Minor variations in fracture morphology among nominally identical specimens may be attributed to local microstructural variation or specimen extraction location. Future work will incorporate bulk chemical analysis (C and O) to more rigorously quantify any composition changes associated with graphite-assisted feeding and interfacial oxidation. (Figure  13 ).
Fig. 13 SEM fractography of tensile fracture surfaces: ( a - b ) feedstock, ( c - d ) as-deposited AFSD material, ( e - f ) 210 °C tempered condition, and ( g - h ) 518 °C tempered condition

sections.heading: AFSD process optimization and deposition behavior
paragraphs: Optimizing the process parameters showed that CS1018 has a narrow AFSD processing window for defect-free deposition. When using higher layer thickness (1 mm) and feed rates, there was excessive flash and poor bonding. In contrast, optimized settings (0.5 mm layer, 0.4 mm/s feed, 2.7 mm/s traverse) produced smooth, continuous deposits, showing how sensitive steel AFSD is to heat input and material balance [ 21 ,  22 ]. During the AFSD build, steady torque, force, and temperature confirmed adequate frictional heating and plasticization, which matches earlier findings on friction stir-based additive manufacturing of steels [ 23 ,  24 ]. The temperature near the substrate stabilized around 580 °C, which was enough to maintain metallurgical bonding without overheating the substrate, though temperatures directly under the tool were likely much higher [ 25 ].

The results indicate that the deposition quality was highly sensitive to the combination of layer thickness, feed rate, and traverse speed. Higher material input promoted flash formation and surface irregularities, whereas lower feed rates improved material flow stability and deposit uniformity. Similar trends have been reported in recent AFSD studies, where balancing material input and thermomechanical processing was found to be critical for achieving defect-free deposits and consistent interlayer bonding [ 3 ,  8 ]. The optimized condition used in this study provided stable deposition with reduced flash and improved surface quality.

sections.heading: Microstructure-property relationships
paragraphs: The AFSD process changed the coarse ferrite–pearlite structure of the cold-drawn feedstock into a much finer microstructure. Ferrite grain size decreased from about 5 μm to 3 μm, and the pearlite fraction increased from 17% to 31%. This refinement, caused by strong plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization, is similar to what is seen in other ferrous alloys processed by AFSD [ 26 ,  27 – 28 ]. No martensitic phases were found, which shows that the low carbon content (0.15–0.20 wt%) and the heat profile prevent martensite from forming. This sets CS1018 apart from medium- and high-carbon steel processing, where martensite often forms [ 29 ].

The mechanical properties changed after AFSD, with about an 18% drop in hardness and a 10–11% decrease in tensile strength, but a 78% increase in elongation. This shift shows the move from a work-hardened feedstock to a fine-grained, annealed-like ferrite–pearlite structure. These changes favor ductility and toughness over strength, making AFSD CS1018 a good choice for uses where damage tolerance and energy absorption are important [ 30 ,  31 ]. Although grain refinement generally increases strength through Hall–Petch strengthening, the AFSD process also removes the cold-work strengthening present in the feedstock and promotes recovery and recrystallization. The reduction in dislocation density outweighs the strengthening contribution from grain refinement, resulting in a net decrease in hardness and tensile strength. This behavior is consistent with the transition from a cold-drawn feedstock to a fine-grained ferrite–pearlite microstructure with reduced stored deformation energy. Lüders band-type serrated yielding was seen in AFSD samples, showing that the fine ferrite grain structure still blocks dislocation motion, which is typical for fine-grained low-carbon steels [ 32 ,  33 – 34 ].

Tempering after deposition at 210 °C and 518 °C caused only small changes. XRD peak narrowing after tempering shows stress relief and lattice recovery, but no major phase changes. The 210 °C treatment gave mild stress relief with almost no change to the microstructure, while the 518 °C treatment caused slight pearlite coarsening and more grain growth (to about 3.7 μm), but kept the refined ferrite–pearlite structure [ 35 ,  36 ]. Fractography showed fine, evenly spread dimples in all AFSD samples, while the feedstock had larger dimples. This supports the improved ductility and toughness from the refined microstructure [ 37 ].

sections.heading: Interfacial bonding and oxidation effects
paragraphs: While the centers of AFSD layers showed strong metallurgical bonding, small areas with poor bonding and higher oxygen levels at the edges suggest that local oxidation can weaken bonding near the edges. These edge areas get less effective forging and more exposure to air, so thin oxide films can remain and reduce metal-to-metal contact. Similar oxidation problems have been seen in friction stir-based additive manufacturing of ferrous alloys, where oxide films at interfaces can cause kissing bonds and delamination [ 38 ,  39 – 40 ].

Tempering did not fix these existing edge defects, showing that heat treatment after deposition alone cannot solve interfacial problems caused by oxidation or not enough local forging. This study did not include bulk chemical analysis for carbon and oxygen, which limits how well we can measure carbon pickup from graphite lubricant and oxidation during AFSD. Other studies have found that graphite-based lubricants can cause carbon to build up at layer boundaries, which may affect the pearlite fraction and interfacial properties [ 41 ]. Future work should include bulk carbon and oxygen measurements, direct residual stress measurements using XRD or neutron diffraction, and more detailed study of edge-region properties to better understand how oxidation and carbon movement affect bonding and mechanical performance.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study demonstrated that CS1018 low-carbon steel can be successfully fabricated by AFSD, producing a dense build with continuous layers and no large-scale lack-of-bond defects observed in the central regions. Microscopy revealed only minor interfacial features in the central regions, such as thin and distributed bond-line oxides, which are encouraging from a bonding standpoint. However, small edge cracks and poorly bonded regions were observed near the deposit boundaries, and these defects become more pronounced toward the edges. While the central portion of the deposit shows good integrity and may be suitable for use, further process optimization is required to mitigate edge-related defects to meet the requirements of most service applications.

Tempering at 210 °C and 518 °C promoted recovery and minor pearlite coarsening while preserving a similar ferrite–pearlite microstructure without introducing new defects. However, the pre-existing oxide-lined gaps remained unchanged.

The AFSD-processed CS1018 exhibited mechanical properties characteristic of well-annealed, fine-grained low-carbon steels. The hardness was approximately 18% lower than that of the feedstock, primarily due to the relief of residual stresses and dynamic recovery during processing, rather than work-hardening effects, which are minimal in low-carbon steels. Tensile strength was reduced by ~ 11%, while ductility increased by ~ 78%, reaching a strain of ~ 30%. The more ductile response is associated with the removal of cold-work effects and the formation of a ferrite–pearlite microstructure during AFSD, yielding an ultimate tensile strength of approximately ~ 554 MPa.

Overall, AFSD followed by moderate tempering offers a robust route to produce CS1018 with near-full density, a ferrite–pearlite microstructure and increased ductility compared to the feedstock. Tempering provides microstructural stability and promotes recovery without significantly degrading mechanical properties or interlayer bond quality, aside from the minor defects that persist at layer edges.
